narration.ages4To6: Mercury is a small, rocky planet covered in craters. This spinning view is made from spacecraft pictures. Some special color pictures help us see different rocks.
narration.ages7To9: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. MESSENGER photographs reveal a rocky surface full of impact craters. Enhanced colors help scientists compare rocks.
narration.ages10To12: Mercury is a terrestrial planet with an ancient cratered surface. This globe is reconstructed from MESSENGER observations; enhanced-color photographs reveal compositional differences, not the colors our eyes would see.

narration.ages4To6: Mercury can be very hot, but some deep craters never see sunlight. Ice can hide in those cold shadows!
narration.ages7To9: Near Mercury's poles, some crater floors stay in permanent shadow. These cold traps can preserve water ice even on a planet so close to the Sun.
narration.ages10To12: Mercury's small axial tilt keeps some polar crater floors permanently shaded. The resulting cold traps preserve water ice; proximity to the Sun alone does not determine every surface temperature.

narration.ages4To6: Look at the bright, shallow pits called hollows. Scientists are still solving the mystery of how they form.
narration.ages7To9: MESSENGER discovered bright hollows in Mercury's rocks. Scientists think material may escape from the surface, leaving shallow pits.
narration.ages10To12: Mercury's hollows are bright, shallow depressions. Loss of volatile material is a leading explanation, but details remain under investigation. Learning science means noticing what is known and what is still uncertain.

narration.ages4To6: Venus wears thick clouds that hide its rocky ground. This landscape is an artist's idea, not a camera picture. Venus is the hottest planet.
narration.ages7To9: Venus is a rocky planet hidden by thick clouds. This NASA landscape is an artist's concept. Its dense atmosphere traps so much heat that Venus is hotter than Mercury.
narration.ages10To12: Venus has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and an extreme greenhouse effect. The landscape is a NASA artist's concept, not direct footage. Surface temperatures average about 465 degrees Celsius.

narration.ages4To6: How can we peek through the clouds? Spacecraft use radar! This color picture made with radar shows a volcano.
narration.ages7To9: Magellan sent radar through Venus's clouds and mapped mountains and volcanoes. Colors in this radar map were added to help us study the terrain.
narration.ages10To12: Magellan mapped Venus with radar, which penetrates the cloud deck. This assigned-color radar visualization shows volcanic landforms; its displayed colors do not represent a visible-light photograph.

narration.ages4To6: Venus is almost as wide as Earth, but it is a very different home. Its thick, hot air would not be safe for us.
narration.ages7To9: Venus is nearly Earth-sized, yet its atmosphere and surface conditions are very different. It also spins slowly in the opposite direction from most planets.
narration.ages10To12: Similar size does not guarantee similar environments. Venus's slow retrograde rotation, dense atmosphere and greenhouse heating distinguish it from Earth. Comparing planets helps scientists test explanations for their histories.

narration.ages4To6: Earth turns like a spinning ball. The side facing the Sun has day, and the other side has night. This moving globe is a model made with real Earth pictures.
narration.ages7To9: Earth rotates about once every day. As places turn toward or away from sunlight, they move between day and night. This globe is a visualization, not a live camera.
narration.ages10To12: Earth's rotation changes which hemisphere receives sunlight, producing day and night. This NASA visualization combines surface imagery, clouds, atmosphere and city lights; motion is sped up for learning.

narration.ages4To6: Earth has blue oceans, white clouds, and land. More of its surface is ocean than land. Earth is the only world where we know life lives.
narration.ages7To9: Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth's surface. Liquid water, an atmosphere and many other conditions support life. Earth remains the only planet with confirmed life.
narration.ages10To12: About 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by ocean. Interactions among water, air, rocks and living organisms shape our planet. Liquid water is important for life as we know it, but is not proof of life on another world.

narration.ages4To6: Those glowing ribbons are auroras! Tiny bits from space meet Earth's upper air and make beautiful lights.
narration.ages7To9: Auroras appear when energetic particles interact with gases high in Earth's atmosphere. Earth's magnetic field helps guide particles toward polar regions.
narration.ages10To12: Energetic particles excite gases in the upper atmosphere, which release light as auroras. Earth's magnetic field influences where particles arrive, connecting visible polar lights with the Sun-Earth space environment.

narration.ages4To6: Saturn is a giant planet with clouds. Near its north pole, clouds make a six-sided pattern! These old spacecraft pictures show its colors changing.

narration.ages10To12: Saturn's north-polar hexagon is an atmospheric pattern. This comparison uses Cassini observations from 2013 and 2017. Seasonal illumination and atmospheric haze can alter the polar region's color.

narration.ages4To6: Saturn's bright rings are not one big solid hoop. They are made of countless little pieces of ice and rock going around the planet.
narration.ages7To9: Saturn's rings contain many separate orbiting particles, mostly water ice with rocky material. The particles range from tiny grains to large chunks.
narration.ages10To12: Saturn's rings are a disk of independently orbiting particles, dominated by water ice. Their structure includes ringlets, gaps and waves influenced by gravity and interactions with moons.

narration.ages4To6: Cassini sent home wonderful pictures of Saturn. Far away in one picture, Earth looks like a tiny dot!
narration.ages7To9: Cassini explored Saturn, its rings and moons from 2004 to 2017. In the Day the Earth Smiled image, our home is a tiny distant point.
narration.ages10To12: Cassini's 2004–2017 orbital mission transformed knowledge of Saturn's atmosphere, rings and satellites. The Day the Earth Smiled mosaic illustrates perspective: apparent size changes with viewing distance.

narration.ages7To9: Uranus is an ice giant with an axis tilted about 98 degrees. This NASA animation shows a model of the planet; it is not live spacecraft footage.
narration.ages10To12: Uranus is an ice giant with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees. The NASA conceptual animation is a model, not direct footage. Extreme tilt creates unusual seasonal illumination.

narration.ages4To6: Methane gas in Uranus's air takes away some red light. More blue-green light reaches our eyes. Special camera colors can show clouds more clearly.

narration.ages10To12: Voyager 2's 1986 flyby provided the only close spacecraft encounter with Uranus. Combining those measurements with telescopic observations helps scientists investigate its atmosphere, ring system, moons and magnetic environment.

source.title: NASA SVS: Neptune: A Faraway Weather Adventure

narration.ages4To6: Neptune is the eighth planet and the farthest planet from the Sun. This spinning view is a model made from spacecraft pictures.
narration.ages7To9: Neptune is the eighth planet, about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. This rotation-and-tilt visualization is sped up; the planets are not shown at their real distances.
narration.ages10To12: Neptune is the outermost of the eight planets, averaging about 30 astronomical units from the Sun. This reconstructed globe illustrates rotation and tilt; its scale and motion are simplified for presentation.

narration.ages4To6: Neptune has clouds, storms, and very fast winds! This old Voyager picture shows a storm that later went away. Pictures can use stronger colors to help us see details.
narration.ages7To9: Neptune's winds can exceed 2,000 kilometres per hour. The Great Dark Spot in this 1989 Voyager photograph later disappeared. Processed color can make clouds and storms easier to compare.
narration.ages10To12: Neptune's atmosphere supports powerful zonal winds and transient dark vortices. The 1989 Great Dark Spot later disappeared. Displayed hue depends on atmospheric haze and image processing as well as methane absorption.

narration.ages4To6: Neptune takes a very long trip around the Sun. One Neptune year lasts about 165 Earth years!
narration.ages7To9: Neptune orbits the Sun in about 165 Earth years. Light from the Sun takes about four hours to reach it. A faraway planet can still have busy weather.
narration.ages10To12: Neptune's orbital period is about 165 Earth years. Sunlight takes roughly four hours to cross its average solar distance. Its dynamic atmosphere shows that distance from the Sun is not a complete explanation of weather.
